title: Police investigating report of antisemitic hate crime at English school’s under-15 game
content:
Police are investigating following a report of a hate crime during a football match involving Britain’s largest Jewish school in a national tournament.

JFS is a Jewish comprehensive secondary school based in north London.

The alleged incident happened on Thursday, March 5, when they played in an away game in the quarter-final stage of the English School’s under-15 competition against Thorpe St Andrew School, based in Norwich.

As first raised by the Campaign Against Antisemitism — a volunteer-led charity dedicated to exposing and countering antisemitism through education — they were said to have been subjected to abusive chants from the opposition team’s fans.

A mother of one of the boys, who wished to remain anonymous because of the sensitive nature of the incident, told The Athletic: “It’s very disappointing. All the boys were all so excited because it was the first time that JFS had made it to the quarter-final of the tournament.

“When they got to the school, they started warming up and that’s when the chants from the spectators started. They started saying ‘Jews, Jews’ all the time and ‘yids’.

“What’s the problem with being a Jew? Why is it a derogatory term?

“They shouted throughout the game. They were saying ‘go back to the gas chambers’, ‘dirty Jew’ and ‘Zionist’,” she claimed. “It obviously makes you very upset. Over time, these things have a very negative impact on us. We don’t need to hear these things.

“Everybody just tried to get on with it, but why get on with it? Especially in these days now, where antisemitism is exploding everywhere around us. Why do we need to tolerate it? We need to do the opposite, we need to stop it, we need to tackle it, to talk about it.

“Some of the boys were very upset when they got back home. They were sad, hurt and angry. Some of the boys were shocked. Some of them felt ashamed to be Jewish.”

She also claimed one of the JFS boys, who is mixed-race, was called an “N-word Jew”.

In messages, shared with The Athletic, the boys said they felt “threatened”, “really disappointed” and “upset”.

One said: “Hearing those kinds of comments was hurtful and embarrassing, and it made what should have been an enjoyable experience very difficult.”

Another said: “We got there and were trying to warm up but we couldn’t because we were so distracted by the antisemitism. The whole game we couldn’t concentrate on playing football because there were comments and it stopped us from playing, and it got in our heads.”

Thorpe St Andrew School won the match 4-1, knocking JFS out of the competition.

When contacted by The Athletic, a spokesman for Norfolk Police confirmed they received a report of a hate crime on Friday morning.

They said: “The incident happened during a football match, held on Thursday 5 March on Laundry Lane, Thorpe St Andrew, where antisemitic chants were heard coming from spectators. Enquiries are ongoing.”

A spokesperson for the English Schools’ Football Association (ESFA) told The Athletic they were also investigating.

“As this is an ongoing investigation, we are not in a position to comment further at this time,” they added.

In a letter, seen by The Athletic, the safeguarding lead and deputy principal of Thorpe St Andrew School said they “take all matters relating to discrimination, including antisemitic comments and abuse, very seriously.”

They said the incident was being investigated and that the school was liaising with Dr David Moody, the headteacher of JFS.

A spokesman for the academy trust, that includes Thorpe St Andrew, told the Telegraph: “Clearly, antisemitic behaviour of any kind is completely unacceptable and runs counter to the culture and values at our school. We are taking this extremely seriously and have launched a full investigation into the concerns raised.

“We work hard to create a culture of respect in which everyone feels welcome at Thorpe St Andrew, and we are deeply concerned to hear about the comments reported. We will investigate this fully and take action where necessary.”

Elsewhere, in a letter seen by The Athletic, Dr Moody told parents the school will collect statements from all those involved, before contacting Thorpe St Andrew School and ESFA.

“The team has done the school extremely proud going so deep into the competition and they should never have had to put up with the abuse that was thrown at them,” he added.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Campaign Against Antisemitism told The Athletic: “There is no excuse for this kind of outrageous and potentially criminal behaviour.

“We urge the police to investigate and any offenders must face the full force of the law.

“The school too must probe what has happened and take urgent educational steps. We cannot allow tropes like these to become normalised in British schools.”
